title: Make the constraints work together.
card_title: Joint spectral constraints for W4A4 training
question: Can a joint spectral update reduce the W4A4-to-BF16 loss gap beyond normalizing weights after each update?
problem: A small update does not guarantee a well-scaled weight matrix. In low-bit training, accumulated gain drift can amplify activation and quantization error.

insights.title: Choose an update using matrix geometry
insights.text: Spectral steepest descent controls the matrix update. A weight constraint can also change which directions are feasible.

insights.title: Update scale and weight scale are different
insights.text: Controlling a single step does not automatically control the accumulated amplification of the current weights.

connection: Put the weight constraint inside the direction-finding problem. Then ask whether this existing coupling helps the actual quantized computation.
initial: Combine spectral descent with a fixed weight spectral norm.
finding: SSO already makes this combination. It cannot be claimed as a new optimizer.
revision: Narrow the question to W4A4: does joint direction selection help more than post-update normalization, at equal cost?
neighbors: Controlled LLM Training on Spectral Sphere
Quest: Stable training of llms with 1-bit weights and activations
TetraJet-v2: Accurate NVFP4 Training for Large Language Models with Oscillation Suppression and Outlier Control
mechanism: Solve for a spectral-bounded update tangent to the weight spectral sphere, then retract to the target radius. Compare how the resulting geometry affects dequantized weights, activations, and loss.
equation: maximize ⟨M, Φ⟩  subject to ‖Φ‖₂ ≤ 1 and ⟨u₁v₁ᵀ, Φ⟩ = 0
contribution: A mechanism study of when joint spectral constraints improve low-precision training, separating the coupling from normalization and quantizer effects.
validation: Compare Muon, Muon followed by normalization, SSO, and reference optimizers under BF16, W4A16, W16A4, and W4A4. Match both tokens and wall-clock budgets; measure the quantization loss gap and actual numerical error.
failure: The hypothesis weakens if only the master weights stabilize, normalization explains all gains, or solver overhead removes the advantage.
critique: Separate gains from better BF16 optimization from gains specific to quantization. Include equal-wall-clock comparisons.
blueprint: Pin the quantizer, spectral radius, and numerical formats.
Verify tangency and retraction on small matrices.
Measure master-weight and dequantized-weight behavior separately.
Run the precision-by-optimizer comparison with matched budgets.
blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.

title: Treat compression choices as updates.
question: Can legal rounding and pruning choices adapt a pretrained model to a task without adding free floating-point weights?
problem: Good models near a checkpoint in continuous weight space may not be reachable through a fixed low-bit codebook and sparse deployment budget.

insights.title: Use task feedback to select perturbations
insights.text: Forward evaluations can guide adaptation without a full backward graph. The candidate model must still be executable.

insights.title: Compression operations interact
insights.text: The quality of separate compression choices does not determine the quality of their combination, and testing candidates costs queries.

connection: Transfer candidate generation and feedback from perturbation search to legal mask swaps and adjacent rounding choices. Keep the deployment budget fixed throughout.
initial: Adapt a model by choosing quantization and pruning operations using forward-only task feedback.
finding: Mask learning, quantization-parameter tuning, discrete-code updates, and forward-only sparse adaptation already have direct prior work.
revision: Study the restricted reachable set and whether reproducible mask–rounding interactions improve equal-query search efficiency.
neighbors: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
Pv-tuning: Beyond straight-through estimation for extreme llm compression
Maskpro: Linear-space probabilistic learning for strict (n: M)-sparsity on large language models
mechanism: Freeze the checkpoint, scales, and bit widths. Search binary masks and adjacent rounding endpoints through feasible support swaps, rounding flips, and their joint edits. Use task loss to accept candidates.
contribution: Characterize when useful adaptation is reachable through compression alone, and when interaction-guided search earns its additional query cost.
validation: Compare independent edits, sequential compression, random joint search, and interaction-guided search at equal query and deployment budgets. Separate search, selection, and test data; compare against the original base model.
failure: Restoring only the base model's quality is compression recovery. Gains that require an ensemble, extra storage, or repeated test-set queries do not establish the proposed single-model adaptation.
critique: Distinguish recovery of compression loss from adaptation beyond the original model. Count the cost of all four interaction evaluations.
blueprint: Enumerate the legal representation and account for masks, scales, and restoration metadata.
Estimate useful-candidate density before building a complex searcher.
Test whether interaction estimates replicate on fresh batches.
Measure held-out task gain and deployment cost for one final model.
blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.

title: Must every backward pass be accurate?
question: Can occasional matched-state reference replay correct cheap compressed backpropagation while every execution branch fits a hard memory limit?
problem: Activation compression reduces storage but can bias the final gradient. Exact recomputation costs time and can violate the memory limit on the very steps that need it.

insights.title: Randomize an estimator, not its claim
insights.text: Randomized differentiation trades memory for estimator variance. Correct scaling matters; occasional exact steps alone do not remove bias.

insights.title: Plan compression and recomputation together
insights.text: Saved activations, reconstruction, and approximation offer different memory–computation–error tradeoffs.

connection: Correct the complete gradient residual with inverse-probability weighting, then plan a replay path that is feasible even on rare correction steps.
initial: Use cheap compressed gradients most of the time and occasionally replay the reference calculation.
finding: Randomized AD and activation compression already relax per-step fidelity. The inverse-probability identity is established, and an unbiased gradient does not preserve Adam's second moments.
revision: Focus on the joint replay probability, compression level, and rematerialization schedule, including variance and optimizer-state effects.
neighbors: GACT: Activation Compressed Training for Generic Network Architectures
Checkmate: Breaking the memory wall with optimal tensor rematerialization
mechanism: Keep parameters, data, randomness, and mutable state matched. With known probability p, reconstruct a reference gradient and apply the weighted residual to the compressed gradient. Release intermediate state before replay.
equation: ĝ = gᶜ + (B / p)(g − gᶜ),  B ∼ Bernoulli(p)
contribution: A feasible cost–quality policy for complete residual correction under hard peak-memory constraints, or a precise account of when it cannot help.
validation: Check the conditional gradient mean and covariance at a fixed checkpoint. Measure every branch's peak memory. Compare checkpointing, ActNN/GACT, mixed precision, periodic uncorrected replay, and corrected replay under matched time and reference calls.
failure: The proposal fails if reference replay does not fit memory, state cannot be reproduced, rare corrections destabilize training, or higher precision offers a better equal-time frontier.
critique: Do not equate unbiased gradients with unchanged Adam dynamics. Test SGD first and report correction-step peak memory, not just average usage.
blueprint: Define the reference numerical implementation and replayable state.
Verify the estimator on an enumerable model.
Implement an executable checkpoint/replay schedule under a hard limit.
Measure the time-to-quality frontier and isolate nonlinear optimizer effects.
blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.

title: Is the weight moving—or the scale?
card_title: Separating weight and scale effects in FP4
question: Which FP4 disturbances are caused by master-weight movement, which by shared-scale changes, and which actually affect model outputs?
problem: Threshold crossings depend on W/s. Shared scale changes can move many codes together, so counting code flips can misidentify the source of functional instability.

insights.title: Small updates meet coarse numerical states
insights.text: Dynamic range, lost small updates, and quantization error can affect convergence.

insights.title: Look at the numerical mechanism
insights.text: Weight trajectories, scaling, rounding, and actual dequantized values must be distinguished when analyzing low-bit behavior.

connection: Hold the rest of the computation fixed and cross two adjacent weight states with two scale states. Measure output and loss effects, not only integer labels.
initial: Shared-scale events may be mistaken for individual-weight or optimizer oscillation.
finding: Oscillation, scale sensitivity, and several stabilization methods are already known. A scale-first explanation must be tested against alternatives.
revision: Use four controlled replay conditions to distinguish weight, scale, interaction, and common-cause explanations across quantization formats.
neighbors: Oscillation-free Quantization for Low-bit Vision Transformers
Oscillation-reduced mxfp4 training for vision transformers
mechanism: Replay Q(W₀,s₀), Q(W₁,s₀), Q(W₀,s₁), and Q(W₁,s₁) with fixed inputs and other state. Apply a symmetric two-factor attribution to dequantized tensors, layer outputs, and loss.
equation: Dᵂ + Dˢ = Z₁₁ − Z₀₀;  I = Z₁₁ − Z₁₀ − Z₀₁ + Z₀₀
contribution: A reproducible mechanism diagnosis and evidence for choosing interventions according to their actual cause, rather than another universally claimed stabilizer.
validation: Compare fixed, delayed, and smoothed scales with weight resets and existing oscillation controls. Vary group sizes and formats. Use common randomness and legal crossed states, and track clipping alongside output drift.
failure: Reject scale dominance if scale swaps do not reproduce disturbances, fixing scales does not help, or all gains are explained by one-step quantization error. Code-only changes without output effects are not functional instability.
critique: Treat scale dominance as a competing hypothesis. Do not infer long-term training causality from one replay window.
blueprint: Make neighboring training states fully replayable.
Validate crossed scale settings and record clipping.
Run weight, scale, and common-cause interventions.
Test whether the diagnosed mechanism predicts a useful training intervention.
blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.

title: Compress the verifier. Keep the guarantee.
question: Can compressed target-model state resolve some speculative verification events without changing a specified reference distribution?
problem: Verification can be dominated by long-context cache traffic. Approximate cache states reduce that cost but can also change target probabilities and all later states.

insights.title: The verifier also has a cost
insights.text: Long-context attention and cache traffic make verification itself a resource bottleneck.

insights.title: Preserve the sampling correction
insights.text: Acceptance and rejection correction constrain how verification can be approximated without introducing distribution error.

connection: A guaranteed probability interval can sometimes determine the same random acceptance event. Refine only ambiguous decisions, while handling rejection and future state consistently.
initial: Use compressed verifier state and certify accept/reject decisions with probability intervals.
finding: Compression plus verification and dynamic precision already exist. Correctly accepting one token does not certify residual sampling or the next KV state.
revision: Require three linked guarantees: the current event, the residual distribution after rejection, and all future state-dependent probabilities.
neighbors: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
QuantSpec: Self-Speculative Decoding with Hierarchical Quantized KV Cache
Speculative Verification: Exploiting Information Gain for Speculative Decoding
mechanism: Bound the reference probability by [ℓ,u] and reuse one uniform draw. Decide only when both bounds agree; otherwise refine or restore the reference. Recover exact residual sampling and maintain certified or replayable cache state.
equation: accept if U ≤ min(1, ℓ/q); reject if U > min(1, u/q); otherwise refine
contribution: A useful certificate construction and complete state-consistency argument with an end-to-end cost advantage, or a rigorous boundary showing when that advantage is impossible.
validation: Enumerate small-vocabulary outputs and every acceptance/rejection branch. Construct long-sequence cache-drift counterexamples. Measure certificate tightness, direct-decision rate, replay distance, latency, and peak memory against full verification.
failure: Invalid bounds or incomplete state repair break exactness. Loose bounds and frequent replay can erase savings. Greedy agreement and sample frequencies alone do not prove the distribution guarantee.
critique: Account for residual sampling and future KV consistency, not just the current acceptance decision. Count certificate and repair costs.
blueprint: Specify the numerical reference distribution and sampling transformations.
Prove the interval decision rule with one reused random draw.
Close the residual-sampling and future-state arguments.
Measure whether valid certificates are cheaper than full verification.
blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.

title: Needed now. Worth keeping later?
question: Can committed and rolled-back speculative branches improve expert-cache decisions without changing the model's routing or verification?
problem: Rejected draft tokens still require expert computation during verification. But their accesses may be poor predictors of which expert pages are useful afterward.

insights.title: Cache value depends on future benefit
insights.text: Expert replication, caching, and scheduling depend on hotspots and marginal utility under memory and bandwidth limits.

insights.title: Verification cost depends on real routing
insights.text: Expert overlap across tokens and execution dynamics shape verification cost; accepted-token counts alone do not explain it.

connection: Separate mandatory execution from future residency. Serve all required experts now; use committed and rollback history only to decide what stays afterward.
initial: Use speculative drafts to predict expert demand, then weight demand by commitment probability.
finding: MoE-SpAc already uses speculative activation utility. AcceptMoE already weights demand by commitment. SpecMD already manages expert lifecycles.
revision: Test whether rollback labels add predictive value for post-verification residency at unchanged routing, beyond those existing signals.
neighbors: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios
AcceptMoE: Commitment-Weighted Self-Sizing Verifier Expert Sets for Efficient MoE Speculative Decoding
SpecMD: A Comprehensive Study On Speculative Expert Prefetching
mechanism: Pin pages until their last current verification use. After the result is known, predict future transfer stalls saved per byte using committed-prefix, rejected-only, and fallback-token features. Misses fetch or wait; they never skip required computation.
equation: required execution = ⋃ experts requested now; retention value = expected future stalls saved / bytes
contribution: Evidence that rollback information improves cache admission beyond access recency, frequency, and lifecycle signals, plus an online benefit without changing target semantics.
validation: Replay identical routing and acceptance traces with fixed cache bytes. Compare LRU/LFU, Least-Stale, speculative-frequency utility, and the proposed policy. Shuffle rollback labels, then measure online stalls, transfers, throughput, and tail latency.
failure: No gain if rejected and accepted branches use the same experts, labels add no predictive value, or scheduling overhead exceeds saved stalls. Gains requiring skipped experts or future information do not support the claim.
critique: Preserve every required expert execution. Compare against equal-information Least-Stale and speculative-utility policies; shuffle rollback labels.
blueprint: Collect unchanged-routing reference traces and acceptance outcomes.
Separate page execution lifetimes from retention decisions.
Ablate commitment/rollback labels on identical traces.
Validate online latency and unchanged model computation at equal memory.
blueprint_note: Suggested development steps summarized from the original proposal; no new experiment is reported.
